extraction.name: Natural Questions
extraction.description: A question answering data set consisting of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine, paired with Wikipedia pages from the top 5 search results and annotated with long answers, short answers, or null when no answer is present.
extraction.creator: Tom Kwiatkowski, Jennimaria Palomaki, Olivia Redfield, Michael Collins, Ankur Parikh, Chris Alberti, Danielle Epstein, Illia Polosukhin, Jacob Devlin, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova, Llion Jones, Matthew Kelcey, Ming-Wei Chang, Andrew M. Dai, Jakob Uszkoreit, Quoc Le, Slav Petrov
extraction.citeAs: Kwiatkowski, T., Palomaki, J., Redfield, O., Collins, M., Parikh, A., Alberti, C., Epstein, D., Polosukhin, I., Devlin, J., Lee, K., Toutanova, K., Jones, L., Kelcey, M., Chang, M.-W., Dai, A. M., Uszkoreit, J., Le, Q., & Petrov, S. (2019). Natural Questions: A Benchmark for Question Answering Research. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 7, 453–466. https://doi.org/10.1162/tacl_a_00276
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions were sampled from real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. All questions were 8 words or more and selected using heuristics intended to filter non-questions while retaining factual questions. Questions were kept when a Wikipedia page appeared in the top 5 search results. Human annotators were then presented with a question and Wikipedia page pair and completed three stages in succession: question identification as good or bad, long answer identification by selecting the earliest HTML bounding box containing enough information to infer the answer or marking no answer, and short answer identification by selecting one or more entities within the long answer, yes/no, or no short answer.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Both the long and short answer can be NULL if no viable candidates exist on the Wikipedia page. Annotators mark no answer if the page does not answer the question or if the information is present but not contained in a single allowed element. The paper states that annotators identify a long answer for 49% of examples and short answer spans or a yes/no answer for 36% of examples, and that the remaining 51% with no answer labeled are not discarded.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data sources are real anonymized, aggregated Google search queries and Wikipedia pages returned in the top 5 Google search results for those queries.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Simple heuristics were used to filter questions from the query stream. The authors sampled queries of 8 words or more matching specified syntactic patterns, ran them through Google search, and kept only those with a Wikipedia page in the top 5 results.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions were filtered using heuristics to discard a large proportion of non-questions while retaining most longer questions. Part of speech tags and entities were identified using Google's Cloud NLP API for some heuristics. For annotation, the input was a question paired with a Wikipedia page from the top 5 search results.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotation was performed using a custom annotation interface by a pool of around 50 annotators. The guidelines and tooling divided annotation into three stages completed by a single annotator in succession: determining whether the question was good or bad based only on the question text; for good questions, selecting the earliest HTML bounding box on the Wikipedia page containing enough information to infer the answer or marking no answer; and for examples with long answers, selecting the entity or set of entities within the long answer that answer the question, or marking yes, no, or no short answer. Comprehensive guidelines were developed and annotation quality was constantly monitored. The public release contains single annotations for training and 5-way annotations for development and test; the paper also analyzes 25-way annotations on a subset.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper evaluates annotation quality using post hoc expert evaluation and k-way annotations. Four experts independently judged sampled annotations as Correct, Correct but debatable, or Wrong, then met to reach consensus. Long/short answers had 90%/84% precision respectively when Correct and Correct but debatable were counted as high-quality. The paper also collected 25-way annotations on 302 examples to study variability, showing disagreement about whether an answer is present and about answer location and span boundaries. The authors report that the most popular long answer accounts for 83% of long answer annotations and the two most popular long answers account for 96%; for short answers, the most popular answer accounts for 64% and the three most popular account for 90%.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 for training examples; 5 for development and test examples; 25 for a subset of 302 examples used for variability analysis
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: A pool of around 50 annotators; four experts who had prepared the annotation guidelines were used for post hoc correctness judgments
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that open-domain question answering has significant utility to users and argues that because a solution to Natural Questions will have genuine utility, it is well equipped as a benchmark for natural language understanding.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that the questions are real queries from people seeking information and that the dataset focuses on longer queries because they are more complex. It also states that the dataset focuses on Wikipedia as a source of factual information and that, like any data set, there may be biases in this choice. The authors note that future data collection may introduce shorter queries, "how to" questions, or domains other than Wikipedia.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited to queries of 8 words or more selected by heuristics, excludes many shorter queries and "how to" questions, and uses only Wikipedia pages appearing in the top 5 Google search results. The paper notes biases from focusing on Wikipedia and reports substantial ambiguity and variability in whether answers are acceptable and where they are located. It also notes that list-formatted long answers are harder for baseline models.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is proposed as a benchmark for question answering research and to provide large-scale end-to-end training data for QA. The public release consists of 307,373 training examples with single annotations, 7,830 development examples with 5-way annotations, and 7,842 sequestered test examples with 5-way annotations. The task is to predict a long answer from a Wikipedia page or indicate no answer, and a short answer where applicable.
